claims.text: Resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings is governed by multilayer interfaces acting as barriers to dislocation motion.
Lattice distortions at multilayer interfaces hinder dislocation nucleation.
Elastic mismatches at multilayer interfaces hinder dislocation propagation.
Hindering dislocation nucleation and propagation slows creep.
The proposed multilayer coatings contain alternating high-entropy-alloy layers with distinct lattice parameters and elastic properties.
Homogeneous single-phase high-entropy-alloy coatings lacking multilayer interfaces can serve as the comparison group.
Dislocation-mediated plasticity is dominant under the proposed ambient-to-moderately-elevated-temperature sustained-load conditions.
Interface regions act as dislocation traps because of mismatched lattice parameters and elastic moduli.
Interface-induced strain fields create barriers that impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion enhances resistance to the time-dependent accumulation of plastic deformation.
The high-entropy composition intensifies local lattice distortions and amplifies interface-mediated dislocation blocking.
Multilayer coatings will exhibit lower creep rates than homogeneous high-entropy-alloy coatings tested identically.
Multilayer coatings will have lower dislocation density after prolonged loading than homogeneous high-entropy-alloy coatings.
Multilayer coatings will retain hardness better than homogeneous high-entropy-alloy coatings after prolonged loading.
The mechanism remains effective while multilayer interfaces are chemically sharp.
The mechanism remains effective below temperatures at which diffusion or interface relaxation significantly erodes dislocation blocking.
At very high temperatures or extreme loads, mechanisms other than interface-mediated dislocation blocking may dominate.
The contributions of residual stress and diffusive interface healing, and the interface coherence required for optimal performance, are quantitatively uncertain.
A controlled creep comparison can test the hypothesis by holding stress, temperature, processing, and test duration constant while varying multilayer versus homogeneous architecture.

Failure to observe statistically significant reductions in creep rate and dislocation accumulation, or superior retained mechanical properties, in multilayer coatings would falsify the proposed mechanism.
